source.text: The migration-period peoples who later coalesced into a "German" ethnicity were the Germanic tribes of the Saxons, Franci, Thuringii, Alamanni and Bavarii. These five tribes, sometimes with inclusion of the Frisians, are considered as the major groups to take part in the formation of the Germans. The varieties of the German language are still divided up into these groups. Linguists distinguish low Saxon, Franconian, Bavarian, Thuringian and Alemannic varieties in modern German. By the 9th century, the large tribes which lived on the territory of modern Germany had been united under the rule of the Frankish king Charlemagne, known in German as Karl der Große. Much of what is now Eastern Germany became Slavonic-speaking (Sorbs and Veleti), after these areas were vacated by Germanic tribes (Vandals, Lombards, Burgundians and Suebi amongst others) which had migrated into the former areas of the Roman Empire.
source.title: Germans

source.text: Charlemagne's court in Aachen was the centre of the cultural revival sometimes referred to as the "Carolingian Renaissance". Literacy increased, as did development in the arts, architecture and jurisprudence, as well as liturgical and scriptural studies. The English monk Alcuin (d. 804) was invited to Aachen and brought the education available in the monasteries of Northumbria. Charlemagne's chancery—or writing office—made use of a new script today known as Carolingian minuscule,[M] allowing a common writing style that advanced communication across much of Europe. Charlemagne sponsored changes in church liturgy, imposing the Roman form of church service on his domains, as well as the Gregorian chant in liturgical music for the churches. An important activity for scholars during this period was the copying, correcting, and dissemination of basic works on religious and secular topics, with the aim of encouraging learning. New works on religious topics and schoolbooks were also produced. Grammarians of the period modified the Latin language, changing it from the Classical Latin of the Roman Empire into a more flexible form to fit the needs of the church and government. By the reign of Charlemagne, the language had so diverged from the classical that it was later called Medieval Latin.
source.title: Middle Ages

source.text: Sylvester is a name derived from the Latin adjective silvestris meaning ``wooded ''or`` wild'', which derives from the noun silva meaning ``woodland ''. Classical Latin spells this with i. In Classical Latin y represented a separate sound distinct from i, not a native Latin sound but one used in transcriptions of foreign words. After the Classical period y came to be pronounced as i. Spellings with Sylv - in place of Silv - date from after the Classical period.
source.title: Sylvester

EXPERIMENT TASK — WRITE SPARQL FOR MUSIQUE QUESTION

Prompt version: musique-sparql-evidence-first-v1

ROLE

You are constructing the SPARQL computation for a multi-hop question-answering
experiment over a frozen RDF graph.

Your job is not merely to state or force the expected answer.

Your job is to express a query whose ?answer value is obtained by executing
graph patterns against the RDF graph supplied below.

WHY THE QUERY STRUCTURE MATTERS

The query is executed over the frozen graph.

After execution, the computation is traced backwards to determine which RDF
statements contributed to each returned answer, and those RDF statements are
resolved back to their exact source occurrences.

Therefore the answer must genuinely arise from graph matching.

A query that simply injects an already-known answer may return the right value,
but it does not express the computation we need to observe.

THE FROZEN GRAPH IS THE SOURCE OF TRUTH FOR THIS TASK

Every triple pattern you rely on must correspond to relations actually available
in the frozen RDF graph.

Do not invent a relation because it would make the reasoning chain work.

Do not assume a benchmark relation exists unless you can locate the corresponding
RDF triple in the supplied graph.

If the graph does not contain the relation needed for an intended reasoning
step, do not fabricate it.

DECOMPOSITION

The MuSiQue decomposition describes the intended semantic dependency of the
question.

Use it to understand what each reasoning step means and to look for corresponding
relations in the frozen graph.

The decomposition does not create facts in the graph.

An intermediate answer from the decomposition may help you recognize entities,
but the SPARQL computation must still derive its bindings through the graph
relations that actually exist.

CONSTRUCT THE QUERY

Find the RDF triples in the frozen graph that can realize the question.

Use variables to connect dependent graph patterns.

The final ?answer variable must occur in an RDF triple pattern that retrieves
its value from the graph.

Example:

Graph:
    <Organization> <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .

To retrieve the organization represented by FIFA:

    ?answer <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .

Do not instead write:

    <Organization> <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .
    BIND(<Organization> AS ?answer)

The first query derives the answer.
The second query inserts an answer that was already known.

SUPPORTED QUERY FORM

Use a SELECT query with ?answer as the answer variable.

Use basic RDF triple patterns and joins through shared variables.

Do not use:
- BIND
- VALUES
- SELECT DISTINCT
- GRAPH
- SERVICE
- SPARQL updates
- FROM clauses

Python adds dataset scoping after your semantic query is produced.

MATCHED TRIPLES

on while constructing the query.

Copy those N-Triples lines exactly from the supplied frozen graph.

Do not report a triple that is not present in the graph.

{
